fields.title: Three letters and what is between them
fields.keyTakeaway: SLI measures, SLO sets the target, SLA promises to the outside, and the substantive part of the work is not the number, but defining what counts as success.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: An engineer says "our SLO is 99.9%". What does this mean for the product and where did the number come from?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Reliability targets are usually assigned by tradition rather than derived. Too high a target consumes team capacity on things the user will not notice. Too low a target results in a product people do not trust. Both mistakes belong to the PM because the question "how much reliability is needed" is a product question.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: Three concepts built from the bottom up.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **[[sli|SLI]] — what we measure.** A specific metric: share of successfully answered requests; share of responses faster than 500 ms. This is a fact.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **[[slo|SLO]] — internal target.** "Share of successful responses no less than 99.9% over 30 days." An internal decision, not an obligation to anyone.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **[[sla|SLA]] — external promise** with penalties for violation. Always softer than SLO: if you promise 99.9%, you should aim for 99.95%, otherwise any deviation is a contract breach.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: The main thing here is the **definition of [[successful-request|success]]**, not the number. What counts as a failure?
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: *Only error responses?* Then a service taking 30 seconds to reply is formally working, while the product is unusable. *Responses slower than a threshold too?* Then what threshold and on which operations. *Do we count user errors?* A `422` response for a wrong address is not our outage.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: A good SLI is formulated from the user's perspective: **the share of requests that responded correctly faster than N ms, among requests that should have been successful.**
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: Second is the **[[measurement-window|measurement window]]**. 99.9% per month and per week are different promises. 43 consecutive minutes are allowed per month; 10 per week.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Three SLIs defined, based on scenario criticality.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/rows/0/1: Share of successful submits faster than 3 s
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/rows/1/1: Share of responses faster than 1 s
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: Different targets for different scenarios was the main takeaway from this work. Before it, there was a single number for everything, which meant the partner cabinet was defended as dearly as checkout.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: Defining success for checkout was discussed the longest. Agreement reached: success is an order created and the user seeing confirmation faster than three seconds. Rejection due to item unavailability is not a failure, it is correct operation. A timeout is a failure even if the order was eventually created.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: An SLO without monitoring to measure it is an intention, not a target. The first thing done is measurement, and it often turns out that actual reliability differs from perceptions.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: SLI measures, SLO sets the target, SLA promises to the outside, and the substantive part of the work is not the number, but defining what counts as success.
